summary: Indiana is permissive for the roof rat, and there is no species trap. The roof rat is not on any Indiana regulatory list: not a Class I, II, or III animal under the DNR Wild Animal Possession Permit rule (312 IAC 9-11), not an exotic mammal (312 IAC 9-3-18.5), not an endangered mammal (312 IAC 9-3-19), and not a prohibited invasive vertebrate. Under the residual clause 312 IAC 9-3-20, any mammal not identified in the article is an 'exempted wild animal,' which 312 IAC 9-1-6 defines as unprotected and possessable at any time without a permit. The roof rat (R. rattus) and the fancy rat (R. norvegicus) fall into that same residual category by negative taxonomy, so the two are treated identically. Keeping, breeding, and selling or giving are legal with no DNR permit and no state breeder license (Indiana's commercial-breeder law, IC 15-21, is dog-only, and its July 1 2024 retail-pet-store registration defines a retail pet store as selling dogs). Importing a pet roof rat needs no state CVI: the family Muridae is not among the wild families that require an entry CVI under 345 IAC 1-3-4, and rodents are not 'domestic animals' under IC 15-17-2-26. The DNR wild-animal import permit applies only to animals imported for release or sale for release, which does not cover the pet trade. Federal USDA Animal Welfare Act licensing can reach some wholesale or research breeders. Releasing a roof rat is prohibited (312 IAC 9-2-16); local ordinances may add limits.

keep.why: The DNR Wild Animal Possession Permit rule (312 IAC 9-11) requires a permit only for the exhaustively enumerated Class I, II, and III animals (rabbits and native squirrels; furbearers such as beaver, coyote, fox, raccoon, skunk; and dangerous wildlife such as bears, big cats, wolves, venomous reptiles, and large crocodilians). The roof rat and the genus Rattus appear on none of those lists. R. rattus is also absent from the exotic-mammal rule (312 IAC 9-3-18.5, which names 22 families, none of them Muridae) and the endangered-mammal list (312 IAC 9-3-19). Under 312 IAC 9-3-20, any mammal not identified in the article is an 'exempted wild animal,' which 312 IAC 9-1-6 defines as unprotected and possessable at any time. No state permit, facility inspection, registration, or fee is required to keep a roof rat, and the secondary-enclosure and perimeter-fence requirements for Class II and III animals (312 IAC 9-11-10) do not apply.
keep.governing_law: 312 IAC 9-3-20 (exempted wild animal); 312 IAC 9-1-6 (definition); 312 IAC 9-11 (Class I/II/III lists, no Rattus); 312 IAC 9-3-18.5 (exotic mammals, no Muridae); IC 14-8-2-318 (definition of wild animal).

breed.why: Breeding follows keeping. Because the roof rat is an exempted wild animal that needs no possession permit, no DNR permit attaches to breeding it, and the Game Breeder's License (312 IAC 9-10-4) applies only to the listed native furbearers and game species, not to a non-listed pet rodent. Indiana's only commercial-breeder statute, the Commercial Dog Breeder Regulation (IC 15-21), applies solely to dogs, so there is no state breeding license for rats regardless of the number of animals kept or produced. Federal oversight can apply separately: under the USDA Animal Welfare Act, breeders who sell rodents at wholesale or for research, testing, or exhibition may need a USDA Class A or B license, while those who sell only at retail face to face to the final owner are generally exempt.
breed.governing_law: IC 15-21 (Commercial Dog Breeder Regulation, dogs only); 312 IAC 9-10-4 (Game Breeder's License, listed species only); 312 IAC 9-3-20 (exempted wild animal). Federal: USDA Animal Welfare Act (7 U.S.C. 2131 et seq.).

sell_give.why: No Indiana statute licenses or restricts selling or giving away pet rodents. The sale of an exempted wild animal is not permitted, tracked, or taxed by the DNR (the only limit being that animals may not be sold for release into the wild). The July 1 2024 retail-pet-store and animal-care-facility registration added to IC 15-21 defines a 'retail pet store' as a business that sells dogs, with sourcing rules targeting dog sellers, so a seller dealing only in roof rats, fancy rats, mice, or other small rodents is outside that scheme and need not register with the Board of Animal Health. Sellers are not required to provide a state health certificate, origin documents, or microchips. Federal USDA Animal Welfare Act dealer licensing can apply to some commercial sellers (wholesale or to research, testing, or exhibition).
sell_give.governing_law: IC 15-21 (retail pet store defined as selling dogs); 312 IAC 9-3-20 (exempted wild animal); 312 IAC 9-2-16 (no sale for release). Federal: USDA Animal Welfare Act (7 U.S.C. 2131 et seq.).

transport.why: In-state transport is unregulated. For import into Indiana, no state CVI is required for a pet roof rat: 345 IAC 1-3-4 requires an entry CVI for 'domestic animals' (a list in IC 15-17-2-26 that omits rodents) and, for wild animals, only for the families bovidae, camelidae, cervidae, equidae, and suidae, so the family Muridae is not covered. The DNR wild-animal import permit (312 IAC 9-10-20) applies only to a mammal imported for release or sale for release in Indiana, which does not include the pet trade. No state entry permit or border health test is mandated to bring a pet roof rat into Indiana, although a destination state or country may impose its own rules on export, so confirm the receiving jurisdiction's requirements before moving an animal across a border. Releasing a roof rat into the wild is prohibited under 312 IAC 9-2-16.
transport.governing_law: 345 IAC 1-3-4 (entry CVI; Muridae not listed); IC 15-17-2-26 (domestic-animal definition omits rodents); 312 IAC 9-10-20 (wild-animal import permit applies only to import for release/sale for release); 312 IAC 9-2-16 (no release).

restrictions.summary: It is unlawful to release a captive-bred mammal into the wild (312 IAC 9-2-16), and an exempted wild animal may not be sold for release. The roof rat is a non-native species; keep it contained and rehome responsibly, never release it. Local city or county ordinances may independently restrict non-native or exotic pets (for example, some Indiana municipalities define an 'exotic animal' as any species not native to the United States, which would include the roof rat), so check your local code, county zoning, and any HOA covenants.
steps: Never release a roof rat into the wild (312 IAC 9-2-16); rehome, surrender to a rescue, or seek humane euthanasia if you can no longer keep it
Do not sell or transfer a roof rat for release
Check your city and county ordinances and any HOA covenants for local exotic or non-native pet limits before keeping or selling
restrictions.where_to_file: Local code enforcement / county zoning office; Indiana DNR for wildlife questions

inquiry_focus: (1) DNR: written confirmation that captive-bred R. rattus is an 'exempted wild animal' under 312 IAC 9-3-20 (not Class I/II/III under 312 IAC 9-11, not an exotic mammal under 312 IAC 9-3-18.5), requiring no possession, breeding, or game-breeder permit. (2) BOAH: confirmation that a rodent-only breeder or seller is outside the IC 15-21 'retail pet store' definition (which names dogs) and is exempt from BOAH registration and sourcing rules, and that no entry CVI is required for a pet rodent because Muridae is not among the families listed in 345 IAC 1-3-4. Both are confirmation requests; the underlying law already resolves to legal.
